title: Brain connectivity aberrations in anabolic-androgenic steroid users.
response:
This study (PMID: 27942448) investigated the effects of anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) use on brain connectivity in 151 males, including 50 current users, 16 previous users, and 59 controls. The results showed that current AAS users exhibited reduced functional connectivity between key nodes involved in emotional and cognitive regulation, including the amygdala and default-mode network (DMN), and between the dorsal attention network (DAN) and a frontal node encompassing the superior and inferior frontal gyri (SFG/IFG) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). These connectivity aberrations were associated with impulsivity and other behavioral consequences of AAS use, and were further reduced as a function of dependency, lifetime exposure, and cycle state (on/off). 

The findings suggest that AAS use may disrupt brain networks involved in emotional and cognitive regulation, leading to impulsivity and other behavioral problems. The study's results provide evidence for the neurobiological basis of impulsivity in AAS users, and highlight the importance of further research into the neural mechanisms underlying AAS-related behavioral consequences.

title: Role of White Matter Microstructure in Impulsive Behavior.
response:
A recent study published in The Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences (2022) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and white matter microstructure in healthy individuals. The study found that impulsivity, particularly motor and nonplanning impulsiveness, was inversely correlated with whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) values (PMID: 35040662). 

In other words, individuals with higher motor impulsiveness and nonplanning impulsiveness tended to have lower FA values, indicating reduced white matter microstructural integrity. Conversely, higher FA values were associated with nonplanning impulsiveness. These correlations were observed in specific white matter tracts, including the corticospinal tract and the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus.

These findings suggest that impulsivity may be linked to specific white matter microstructural connectivity, supporting the notion that impulsivity is a network-based construct. This study provides initial evidence that altered white matter microstructure may underlie normal individual variability in impulsive behaviors, which could have implications for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity and potentially informing the development of novel interventions.

These findings provide evidence that impulsivity may be linked to altered brain structure in individuals at high risk for bipolar disorder. The study's results suggest that neuroimaging markers, such as FA and MD values in specific white matter tracts, may have potential as biomarkers for early recognition of bipolar disorder.
